explanations.explanation: That's the reason Luke gives: "They were astonished at His teaching, because His message had authority." Jesus wasn't just passing along thoughts. He spoke like His words carried weight. Picture me stamping a cookie and the dough actually obeying. That would astonish me too.

Not quite, friend. The text never says the message was simple. It says they were astonished because "His message had authority" (Luke 4:32). That's the whole reason. I've been called simple myself, but it was never a compliment.

The text says nothing about a language, friend. What astonished the people was this: "His message had authority" (Luke 4:32). Not a fancy tongue, not a special accent. Authority. I'd stay away from guessing on what the Bible doesn't say.

Yes! The man cries out, "I know who You are—the Holy One of God!" (Luke 4:34). He says it loud, right there in the synagogue. He asks, "Have You come to destroy us?" and then he names Jesus. Nobody had to introduce Jesus to that voice.

The text says otherwise, friend. After asking what Jesus wants with them, the man goes on: "I know who You are—the Holy One of God!" (Luke 4:34). So he does say he knows who Jesus is. Easy one to miss, since he was hollering the whole time.
That's it. "Jesus rebuked the demon. 'Be silent!' He said. 'Come out of him!'" (Luke 4:35). Jesus doesn't argue and doesn't debate. He gives two short commands, and the demon has to answer to them.

Not this time, friend. The words came out of a man with an unclean spirit, and Jesus didn't answer with praise. The text says, "Jesus rebuked the demon" (Luke 4:35). He spoke straight to the demon, not to the man's applause line.

Jesus stays right where He is, friend. He doesn't slip out the side door. He says, "Be silent!" and "Come out of him!" (Luke 4:35). Walking out quietly would be me leaving a smoking oven alone. Jesus deals with it on the spot.

I see why you'd think so, since the demon throws the man down in front of everyone. But look at the end of that verse: the demon "came out without harming him" (Luke 4:35). The man was thrown down and left unharmed. That's the actual text, friend.
Right. The demon throws the man down before them all, and it "came out without harming him" (Luke 4:35). It looks scary, but the man isn't hurt. He gets up free. That's a fall worth having.

Yes! The people ask, "With authority and power He commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!" (Luke 4:36). They watched it happen with their own eyes. And remember, a demon had just obeyed Jesus in front of the whole synagogue.

Good thought, friend, because Jesus does that later. But not here. In this scene the people say He commands "the unclean spirits, and they come out!" (Luke 4:36). The wind and waves belong to a different story, so keep that one in your back pocket.

Not in this passage, friend. The people in the synagogue are amazed by what they just saw. They say He commands "the unclean spirits, and they come out!" (Luke 4:36). The sun and moon aren't in the room.

explanations.answer: Jesus is asked to help her
explanations.explanation: That's right. Luke says, "they appealed to Jesus on her behalf" (Luke 4:38). Simon's mother-in-law was suffering from a high fever, and somebody took it straight to Jesus. Good place to take it, friend.
The text doesn't mention a doctor, friend. It says, "they appealed to Jesus on her behalf" (Luke 4:38). Her fever was high, and they went to Jesus about it. Nobody ran off to find anyone else.

explanations.answer: She is left to rest alone
explanations.explanation: No, she wasn't left alone, friend. The people with her "appealed to Jesus on her behalf" (Luke 4:38). They didn't just shut the door and hope for the best. Somebody spoke up for her, and that mattered.

Yes! "She got up at once and began to serve them" (Luke 4:39). No slow recovery, no long nap. The fever left, and she was up. I can't even get out of bed after a cold without three days and a blanket.

A fair guess, friend, but that's not the word. Luke says, "she got up at once and began to serve them" (Luke 4:39). The text says she served. It doesn't tell us whether she said thank you, so I won't add that.
Close in spirit, friend, but not the word. The text says she "got up at once and began to serve them" (Luke 4:39). Serve is the word Luke picked. The fever left, and she got right up.

Not quite, friend. Luke says that "all who were ill with various diseases" were brought to Jesus, and that "laying His hands on each one, He healed them" (Luke 4:40). Not a few. Every one of them. That's a lot of hands and a lot of healing.

That's right. "Laying His hands on each one, He healed them" (Luke 4:40). Each one, friend. Nobody got sent home with just a pat on the back. That's a long line, and Jesus stayed with every person in it.

Yes! Luke says Jesus "would not allow them to speak, because they knew He was the Christ" (Luke 4:41). The demons were shouting, "You are the Son of God!" and Jesus rebuked them. They knew who He was, and He still didn't let them speak.

No, friend. A Pharisee was a member of a religious group, and that's not what the demons knew. The text says, "because they knew He was the Christ" (Luke 4:41). They were shouting that He is the Son of God.

Not this one, friend. The Baptist is a name for John, who baptized people, and he's not who the demons are talking about. Luke says "they knew He was the Christ" (Luke 4:41). Jesus rebuked them and didn't let them speak.

Yes! The crowds "came to Him and tried to keep Him from leaving" (Luke 4:42). They found Him out in a solitary place and didn't want Him to go. I know that feeling. It's how my family felt about my last batch.
Not quite, friend. The crowds weren't trying to stop His preaching. The text says they "tried to keep Him from leaving" (Luke 4:42). They wanted Him to stay right where they were.
Nice try, friend. Nobody was guarding His pillow. Luke says the crowds "tried to keep Him from leaving" (Luke 4:42). He'd gone to a solitary place at daybreak, and they came looking for Him.

explanations.answer: That is why He was sent
explanations.explanation: That's right. Jesus says, "I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well, because that is why I was sent" (Luke 4:43). He gives one reason, and it's about why He was sent. The crowds wanted Him to stay, and He kept to His purpose.
No, friend. The opposite happened. The crowds came looking for Him and tried to keep Him from leaving (Luke 4:42). Jesus says, "that is why I was sent" (Luke 4:43). Capernaum wanted Him to stay.

The text doesn't say that, friend. Jesus gives His own reason: "I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well, because that is why I was sent" (Luke 4:43). No one called Him home. He knew why He was sent.
